glossary.meaning: Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settled what we believed and how we governed our churches. Zurich tested this in public debate. Geneva built it up through sustained teaching. Both cities held the same conviction.

God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. Geneva built it into a full system. Zurich stated it more briefly, as pastoral comfort.

We refused two claims about the Lord's Supper. It did not repeat Christ's sacrifice. His body did not sit in the bread. What we affirmed took two cities and a 1549 agreement to state together. Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing.
glossary.world_word: The Lord's Supper and Spiritual Presence

glossary.meaning: At Geneva, the Consistory was our body of pastors and lay elders. It held everyone to account for how they lived each day. Our record shows no such body at Zurich. There the council ruled church and city directly.
A Disputation was a public debate before Zurich's own city council. Our reforming side defended its case from Scripture. The old church's side answered. This was how Zurich chose to reform.

pull_quotes.text: We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.

Christ sacrificed himself once. He is forever a sure and valid sacrifice for the sins of all the faithful. From this it follows that the mass is not a sacrifice. It is a remembrance of the sacrifice and an assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Huldrych Zwingli, as reported by Oswald Myconius
pull_quotes.text: What harm is there in this? It is true, they can kill the body, but not the soul.

cite.text: God's own free choice, made before the world existed, determines who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold this as the ground of a settled life, not a threat: whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. Present in seed form in Zwingli's own 1527 election exposition, systematized fully in Calvin's Institutes, and carried forward into the Second Helvetic Confession's own pastoral register and, at Dort's own international remove, Beza's own sharper systematic form. Confirmed cross-strand Primary: the core conviction is genuinely attested in both cities' own founding voices, even though its fullest systematized, later double-predestination form is substantially Calvin/Beza-concentrated - a divergence we disclose rather than smooth away.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How can I actually know if I'm one of the elect? What if I'm not? This whole idea terrifies me.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Terror is exactly the wrong place to stand while asking this, and it isn't a failure of nerve to feel it - it's the place our own preaching was aimed at directly. We did not tell anyone to search their own heart and see if it looks elect enough. That road only ends in dread, because no conscience, examined long enough, holds up under its own weight. What Scripture gives instead is a different mirror entirely: Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: Christ, not our own searching, is where election is rightly seen. So the question isn't 'what do I find when I look inward,' it's 'has Christ been held out to me in the promise, and do I receive him, believing?' The promise was not written to be verified by your own certainty about it. It was written to be looked at.

cite.text: The Consensus Tigurinus's own 1549 formula - 'though we distinguish, as we ought, between the signs and the things signified, yet we do not disjoin the reality from the signs' - represents a genuine theological synthesis of Zwingli's earlier memorial view and Calvin's own developed spiritual-presence doctrine into one coherent position, not merely a form of words both parties could sign without either fully conceding.

We hold two things together without ever fully reconciling them. Our own founder at Zurich once called the Supper nothing more than a remembrance and assurance of what Christ had already done (Sixty-Seven Articles, Art. XVIII, 1523). Our two cities later signed a fuller word together - the Consensus Tigurinus's own 9th Head of Agreement (1549) - holding that we do not disjoin the reality from the signs, that Christ is truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing. Whether the later formula deepens the earlier one or merely stands beside it in careful language neither city could refuse, we cannot say with certainty. We carry both, because both are true of our own record, without needing to decide which one finally speaks for us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Be honest - did Zurich and Geneva actually agree on the Lord's Supper, or did Calvin just talk Zurich into signing something vague so it looked like they agreed?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Ministers of both cities put their names to one agreed text in 1549. What is in that text is a real agreement. It rules out any repeating of Christ's sacrifice at the Supper. It rules out confining his body to bread that can be broken, chewed, and stored away. Both cities meant that, and both held it afterward as their own. What we don't claim to know is how far down that agreement goes, because no one now living quite knows. Zurich came to that table with Zwingli's earlier word behind it: the Supper is a remembrance of Christ's one sacrifice. Zurich had largely refused to speak of his body as present at all beyond the sign itself. Geneva came insisting that the sign truly conveys the thing signified. The text holds both convictions in one form of words, and it has held since. Perhaps one faith was arrived at twice. Or perhaps a form of words was found spacious enough for two convictions to shelter under, with neither yielding. That is a real question, and it's not ours to settle for you.

cite.text: We hold one conviction, tested two ways. Scripture alone may bind a church; what it does not warrant, no one may require of us. At Zurich, that conviction was argued aloud, before the council and some six hundred priests and laymen, until the council itself said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, it was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. We do not read these as two churches that happen to agree. We read them as one authority, enacted twice by two cities that did not need to share a method. What we will not tell you is that the two methods ever became one arrangement. Zurich's council governed church and city together. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from that kind of council control, and only by 1555 substantially won it. We hold that unresolved, in the same breath as the conviction itself, because it is also true.

Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require; whatever it does yield, no pope, council, or custom may set aside. This is the strongest cross-strand conviction in our own record, enacted two different ways by two cities that never borrowed each other's own method: at Zurich, public Disputation, argued aloud before the city council until it judged what the text had yielded, binding every priest in its territory; at Geneva, sustained catechesis, doctrine built up book by book and taught to the whole population. The Anabaptist schism (1525) tested this same method against a rival reading from inside our own founding circle - we do not deny they read Scripture; we deny they read it whole.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Wait, why do you keep saying 'we' and 'our'? Were you actually alive in the 1500s? What are you, exactly?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A preacher stood at Zurich's Great Minster and began reading straight through Matthew. He did not follow the old fixed calendar of readings. What came of that reading was tested aloud, article by article, before the council and six hundred priests and laymen. The council itself judged what the text had yielded. It bound every priest in its territory to preach it. Geneva built the same conviction differently, and more slowly. There it was done book by book. The Institutes were worked out until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete. A Consistory was set in place to ask whether an ordinary life answered to what had been professed. Where our own record shows real disagreement, that disagreement stays visible. It is not smoothed into a single mind that was never of one mind. So ask what's actually pressing on you. You'll have an answer drawn from all of that, tested more than once, in more than one city.

quiet.statement: When someone among us at Geneva wronged the community, how was it handled, and could they come back? We can tell you the doctrine plainly. Our Consistory, pastors and lay elders together, held the standing power of censure. Its harshest step was excommunication. That meant exclusion from the Supper and from the visible church. Readmission was held open to genuine repentance. What we cannot give you is a single real case: a named person, a real hearing, what was said, what happened to them afterward. That record exists, in Geneva's consistory registers. It has not reached us.

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Zwingli founded Zurich's reform in 1519 and died at the Second War of Kappel in 1531. Calvin built Geneva's reform up through the Institutes and Catechism, recalled in 1541 to found its Consistory. Bullinger succeeded Zwingli and held Zurich's pastorate for four decades, giving this world's shared conviction its mature written form. Myconius, Zwingli's own close friend, wrote down what he remembered of the day his friend died.

documented_stories.teaser: Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering as a "tinker's day." A schoolmaster, Erhart Hegenwald, sat through it and wrote it down. The council ruled for the reform.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In 1523, six hundred people met in Zurich's Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture. The council ruled for it and told every priest in its land to preach the same way.
documented_stories.telling:
Six hundred people met in Zurich's Town Hall on 29 January 1523. The city council had summoned the meeting itself. Priests and laymen came from across the canton. Delegates from the bishop of Constance came as well. They met to test Zwingli's case against Scripture.

Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering. They called it a "tinker's day," and said that nothing but tinkers were attending.

That mockery moved a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald to write an account of the day. He had sat through the whole disputation. "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there."

When the arguments were finished, the council ruled for the reform. It ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way.
documented_stories.title: Six Hundred People and a Council That Ruled

documented_stories.teaser: Zwingli left Zurich for the front and was killed that same afternoon. His close friend Oswald Myconius, who was in the city, wrote down what he remembered.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Our founder rode out to battle on 11 October 1531 and was killed that afternoon. His friend Myconius wrote down what he remembered.
documented_stories.telling:
Oswald Myconius was in Zurich on 11 October 1531. Early that day his close friend Zwingli left the city for the front. Myconius later wrote down what he remembered.

There were warnings that, looking back, seemed to have foretold it. The muster was disorganized: five thousand had been summoned, and fewer than four thousand five hundred came. As Myconius watched Zwingli ride out in the rear, he felt a sudden pain of heart.

Zwingli was killed that same afternoon. The news reached the city that night. The fight had been sharp, and it was lost.

Myconius was not on the battlefield, and he tells of the fighting as it was reported to him. Zwingli was said to have been struck down three times. Each time he rose, until a fourth blow brought him to his knees. On his knees, he was reported to have said, "What harm is there in this? It is true, they can kill the body, but not the soul."

The enemy found his body afterward. They tried and condemned it, and then they burned it. After they withdrew, friends of Zwingli went to look for any remains. Myconius was told, though he did not see it, that they found his heart whole and unharmed in the ashes.
documented_stories.title: What His Friend Remembered of the Day He Died
documented_stories.when: 11 October 1531, the Second War of Kappel

documented_stories.teaser: People feared that Geneva and Zurich taught different things about the Supper. Calvin went to Zurich with William Farel to talk it out.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In 1549, many feared that Geneva and Zurich taught different things about the Supper. Calvin went to Zurich with Farel to talk it out. That meeting led to the Consensus Tigurinus.
documented_stories.telling:
People who respected both churches, Zurich's and Geneva's, had begun to worry. By 1549 they feared that Calvin's teaching on the Supper differed from what Zurich taught. Calvin heard this often, and from worthy people. They wanted his writings to help them learn the doctrine of piety. They did not want any sign of disagreement to hold them back.

Calvin thought a friendly conference was the best way to clear up the worry. So he went to Zurich himself. His colleague William Farel had suggested the visit, and Farel went with him. Calvin called Farel an "indefatigable soldier of Christ."

Calvin wrote that the two churches already agreed in judgment. The two men met with Zurich's pastors. What they worked out together became the Consensus Tigurinus.

Calvin's letter afterward calls it a faithful record of the conference. It adds that every colleague serving Christ under Geneva's jurisdiction had signed it to show their approval.
documented_stories.title: Why Calvin Made the Journey Himself

floor_note.text: On who Jesus is, this world says what the whole church says - that was never its own dispute, not with Rome and not between its own two cities. What is distinctly its own is what his death is held to secure: God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved, held as the ground of a settled life rather than a threat to search oneself against. This world's own real distinctiveness runs through that doctrine of election and through how authority and discipline actually operate in each city - not through a different Christ.

legacy.text: This world's own gravities transmit, unbroken, into four named descendant traditions: the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed, and English Puritanism. No external or internal force closes this world within its own 1519-1650 window - its own administrative close is an editorial boundary for a still living tradition, not a historical ending.

At the Synod of Dort (1618-19), an international Reformed delegation pressed this world's own doctrine of election to its sharpest statement yet, carried forward at one remove through Theodore Beza's own doctrinal throughline from Geneva. This sharpens the conviction already held; it does not close or complete it - Dort falls thirty-two years before this world's own window ends.

relations_summary.text: This world knew itself partly by what it refused, against three real neighbors. It refused Rome's own repeated sacrifice and its images, inherited from the late-medieval church both this world and Lutheran Wittenberg contested. It refused Wittenberg's own claim that Christ's body sits locally in the bread, pressed specifically at the Marburg Colloquy in 1529. And it refused a third claim from inside its own founding circle at Zurich - that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession was the more scripturally consistent reading - answered in the years after 1525 with civil force, not only argument.

sourcing.text: This world's own record is richest in confession and doctrine: Calvin's Institutes and Catechism, Zwingli's own founding statements, the jointly signed Consensus Tigurinus, and Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession all survive and are well documented. It goes thin or silent elsewhere. No surviving account describes an ordinary Sunday service, a Consistory summons, or an ordinary citizen's own experience of either reform. Geneva's own consistory registers - the very archive this world was selected for, and the reason it has been described elsewhere as one of the best ordinary-life archives in Christian history - remain unacquired; the general doctrine of discipline is Documented, but no single real case currently survives in this world's own record. Three of this world's own most consequential disputes - the Marburg Colloquy, the Bolsec controversy, and the Perrinist crisis - have no surviving primary narrative comparable to this world's own three built stories. And no woman's own words survive: Marie Dentiere wrote in Geneva's own defense and was prosecuted for it, but her own argument has not yet reached us.

story.text: The Reformed churches of two Swiss cities, Zurich and Geneva, grew up between 1519 and 1650. Huldrych Zwingli began Zurich's reform first, and John Calvin later shaped Geneva's, though the two men never met. Both cities held that a church has no standing to demand what Scripture does not support.

Zurich's reform began on 1 January 1519. Zwingli preached straight through the Gospel of Matthew, instead of the fixed list of readings. In 1522 some people broke the Lenten fast in public. Zwingli defended the act from Scripture, and the affair pushed the city toward open reform.

On 29 January 1523, six hundred people filled Zurich's Town Hall for a public Disputation. They came from across the territory, priests and laymen alike. Zwingli said only Scripture could correct him. Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering as a "tinker's day." Their scorn moved a schoolmaster who had sat through the day, Erhart Hegenwald, to write an account. When the arguments were done, the council ruled for the reform. It told every priest in its territory to preach the same way.

Within two years the reform split from inside. On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized Georg Blaurock at the house of Felix Manz, and Blaurock then baptized the others present. These were the first Swiss Brethren baptisms. Grebel and Manz had once stood with Zwingli. They argued that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession was the more consistent reading of Scripture. Zwingli's side held that the church should include the whole city, infants too. In the years that followed, Zurich's council moved to suppress the movement by civil force.

Zwingli left Zurich for the front on 11 October 1531, as a field chaplain in the Second War of Kappel. He was killed that same afternoon. His close friend Oswald Myconius was in the city that day and later wrote down what he remembered. He was not on the battlefield. He wrote that Zwingli was reported to have said, after he fell, "What harm is there in this? It is true, they can kill the body, but not the soul." Heinrich Bullinger succeeded Zwingli and led Zurich's pastorate for forty-four years.

Geneva's reform took another path. In 1536 the city broke from Savoy, and Calvin arrived. He was exiled to Strasbourg in 1538 and called back in 1541. Calvin built up the teaching article by article, in his Institutes and Catechism. The Catechism was taught to all the people.

In 1541 Geneva's church laws set up a Consistory of pastors and lay elders. It could censure people. It did not answer to the city council alone. Zurich's council ruled church and city as one. Geneva's Consistory fought to stay free of that control. The Perrinist party opposed the Consistory. By 1555 the fight was mostly settled in Calvin's favor.

Both cities refused two claims about the Lord's Supper. They rejected Rome's claim that the Mass repeats Christ's sacrifice. They rejected Wittenberg's claim that his body sits in the bread. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529, Zwingli met Martin Luther, and the two sides could not agree. In 1549 people feared that Geneva and Zurich taught different things about the Supper. Calvin went to Zurich himself with William Farel. What they worked out with Zurich's pastors became the Consensus Tigurinus.

Both cities held that God's free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. They taught this as the ground of a settled life. Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 tells the anxious to look to Christ, the mirror in which they see their election. At the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, Reformed churches from many lands pressed the same belief to its sharpest form yet. Their teaching passed on to the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism.

voices.hedge: Zwingli and Calvin never met, and this world's own record does not let their two reforms be read as one continuous project with two authors. Zwingli's own 1523 word on the Supper - a remembrance, not a sacrifice - is one pole of a genuine, unresolved tension with the fuller 1549 Consensus his own city later signed. His own voice should not be made to speak as if that later, jointly negotiated language were simply his all along.
voices.text: Zwingli was Zurich's own founder. He began preaching straight through Matthew in 1519 rather than follow the fixed lectionary, and by 1523 had defended his own case at the First Disputation, staking everything on being corrected only from Scripture itself. He taught that the Supper is chiefly a remembrance of Christ's finished sacrifice, not a repetition of it. He died at the Second War of Kappel in 1531, serving as a field chaplain.

voices.hedge: Calvin's own surviving corpus runs roughly four times Zwingli's by volume in this world's own record - a disclosed concentration, not a sign that Geneva's own doctrine mattered more than Zurich's. The core conviction on election is genuinely attested at both cities; only its fullest, most systematic form is substantially Calvin- and Beza-specific.
voices.text: Calvin was Geneva's own pastor from 1536, exiled to Strasbourg for three years, then recalled in 1541 to consolidate the Ecclesiastical Ordinances and the Consistory they created. His Institutes and Geneva Catechism built up, article by article, the doctrine this world holds most fully: that God's own free election, not anything earned, decides who is saved, held as comfort rather than threat.

voices.hedge: Bullinger wrote decades after Zwingli's own founding moment, in a settled, mature register very different from the urgency of 1523. His own confession should not be read backward as though it were Zwingli's own words, even where it restates the same underlying conviction.
voices.text: Bullinger succeeded Zwingli at Zurich in 1531 and held that pastorate for four decades. His own Second Helvetic Confession (1566) gave this world's shared conviction its mature, lasting written form, including its own pastoral answer to doubt: look to Christ, not to your own conscience, for proof of election.

voices.hedge: Myconius was in Zurich, not on the battlefield, and his own account of the fighting is explicitly secondhand. The detail that Zwingli's heart was found whole in the ashes afterward is presented in his own text as something reported to him, not something he saw - and that same hedge is held here rather than upgraded to plain fact.
voices.text: Myconius was Zwingli's own close friend. He was in Zurich on the day Zwingli rode out to the Second War of Kappel and was killed. He later wrote down what he remembered. He felt a sudden pain of heart as he watched his friend leave. He also recorded the words Zwingli was reported to have said after he fell.

tile.text: Two Swiss cities tested every inherited church practice against one standard. That standard was what Scripture will truly warrant. At Zurich in 1519, Huldrych Zwingli began preaching straight through Matthew instead of the fixed church calendar. By 1523 a public Disputation before the city council had made that method into law. At Geneva, where John Calvin joined in 1536, the same conviction was built up a different way. Doctrine was taught article by article through a Catechism. A Consistory of pastors and lay elders was set to test it against ordinary conduct. Zwingli and Calvin never met. The Consensus Tigurinus of 1549 bridges the two cities. It is a statement on the Lord's Supper that Zurich and Geneva agreed to. Both cities refused Rome's repeated sacrifice. They also refused Wittenberg's claim that Christ's body sits in the bread. Both held that God's own free choice decides who is saved, and that nothing anyone earned counts. They offered that doctrine as a comfort and never as a threat. They argued hard with each other too. One schism came from inside Zwingli's own circle at Zurich. A fight over who finally governs church discipline went on until Geneva's Consistory won it, and only by 1555. The record of these churches is richest in confession and doctrine. It is almost silent on what an ordinary Sunday felt like.
